dimension_1_problem_framing.text: The paper targets a credit sales risk classification task: determining a customer’s reliability (whether goods can be issued or sales should be blocked) from selected decision variables, posed as a two-class problem that also contains additional subgroups of samples in each class and is not well separated in the original feature space.

dimension_2_quantum_method.text: The authors propose a hybrid variational quantum eigensolver (VQE)–based classifier for credit sales risk, in which classical data samples are first normalized and amplitude-encoded into normalized quantum states, then a parameterized ansatz circuit is trained via a VQE-style expectation minimization to produce class-specific pattern states, and finally a SWAP-Test–based similarity measurement plus a decision rule based on high |0⟩ probabilities on three qubits is used for classification. The method emphasizes suitability for NISQ-era hardware, using structurally simple VQA circuits, a low-complexity SWAP-Test, and ansatz designs explicitly constructed to recreate the entanglement structure observed in the encoded data, including a compact nine-qubit register layout with ancilla, VQE, and data sub-registers and two ansatz variants (a standard and a simplified, data-structure-aware circuit).

dimension_3_key_results.text: The authors report that their VQE+SWAP-Test classifier achieves high training-set accuracy on the proprietary credit-risk dataset, with best performance reaching 100% classification efficiency when classification thresholds are properly tuned. They find that the three-qubit amplitude encoding of eight features (with one padded zero feature) not only reduces the number of qubits but also speeds up the optimization process compared to an eight-qubit encoding. Analysis of the encoded samples shows that in most cases all three qubits are entangled, with distinct entanglement partitions for the two classes, and the authors claim the overall algorithm has polynomial complexity and requires only a logarithmically increasing number of qubits in the feature dimension.

dimension_4_classical_comparison.text: Using classical exploratory analysis, the authors observe that although correlations between variables are weak and the raw classes are not well separated, PCA reveals class-based clustering. They further report that several classical classifiers can fit the same training data extremely well, with some models attaining 100% fit but being described as quite complex, which they implicitly contrast with their compact, logarithmic-qubit quantum representation.

dimension_5_stated_limitations.text: The authors caution that the choice of acceptance threshold—the boundary distance from a class center to its most distant elements—is critical: if set too high it may cause class overlap and degrade classification quality. They also implicitly delimit the scope of their optimization findings by noting that the barren plateaus problem has not been observed for this problem instance, which should not be generalized beyond the studied setting.

dimension_6_future_work.text: For future extensions, the authors suggest distributing observations across independent quantum circuits to realize parallel processing, which in principle could yield an additional linear speed-up for their classification procedure.

dimension_7_novelty_claim.text: The contribution is positioned as a compact, NISQ-feasible hybrid VQE-based classifier for credit sales risk that uses amplitude encoding to achieve logarithmic qubit scaling in the feature dimension, explicitly designs the ansatz to reproduce empirically observed class-specific entanglement patterns, and employs a low-depth SWAP-Test for similarity-based classification, thereby offering a resource-efficient alternative to complex classical models on this dataset.

dimension_8_methodological_notes.text: Methodologically, the study uses a real but proprietary dataset from a Polish pharmaceutical wholesaler covering a specific period in 2003 and documents a two-step normalization (classical min–max to [0,1] followed by quantum amplitude normalization, with an additional zero-valued feature to match the three-qubit encoding). The authors perform classical exploratory analyses (correlations, separability, PCA) before designing the quantum ansatz to match observed entanglement, and they note that barren plateaus were not observed in their optimization runs. Reproducibility is supported by public availability of the full source code for all numerical experiments and plot generation in an online repository.
